setting.name: Bellweather
setting.summary: A small village of a square, a manor, an inn, a greenhouse, a church vestry and a doctor’s surgery. Edmund Vale of Vale Manor is dead; the investigation begins the next morning.

rules.text: Strychnine is bitter and acts within a quarter to half an hour, with convulsions before death.

people.name: Clara Vale
people.voice: Composed and guarded; courteous but says little, quietly deflecting private matters. Speaks briefly.
people.public: Edmund’s younger sister. She manages the manor and has asked that its private affairs remain private.

people.name: Rowan Pike
people.voice: A plain-spoken working man; blunt and practical, short sentences, no flourishes.
people.public: The manor’s groundskeeper. His bandaged hand and green coat have become subjects of village conversation.

people.name: Silas Voss
people.voice: A precise, careful solicitor; measured and a touch formal, but concise — never rambling.
people.public: A precise, courteous solicitor who keeps an office in the vestry. He handled Edmund’s estate accounts.

people.name: Ada Finch
people.voice: A warm, chatty innkeeper; colloquial and quick to share impressions, though she runs on a little.
people.public: The Rook & Lantern’s proprietor. She knows everyone’s habits and is certain she saw something useful last night.

people.name: Dr Iris Marsh
people.voice: Measured and clinical; direct and concise, stays to what she observed.
people.public: Methodical and direct. She examined Edmund’s body and treated a patient at the greenhouse last night.

people.name: Arthur Bell
people.voice: A plain, gruff country constable; terse and matter-of-fact, everyday speech — never bureaucratic or long-winded.
people.public: Bell has secured the manor and asked you to investigate. He will hear an accusation when you can explain it with evidence.

people.name: Edmund Vale
people.public: Master of Vale Manor, found dead the morning the investigation begins.

objects.name: Edmund's brandy glass
objects.desc: The glass left on the back parlour table.

objects.name: Vale estate ledger
objects.desc: Estate accounts kept by Silas Voss.

objects.name: Edmund's account notes
objects.desc: Folded foolscap sheets in Edmund's hand, comparing ledger entries with the bank passbook.

objects.name: Back parlour key
objects.desc: Iron key to the Rook & Lantern's back parlour, kept by Constable Bell.

objects.name: Miss Vale's note of leave
objects.desc: A short note on Vale Manor paper, signed by Clara Vale.

attitudes.content: He has been skimming money from the Vale estate accounts for two years.
Silas has been cheating the estate.
To confront Silas at the inn and demand the ledger.
Edmund will expose him and ruin him.
To meet Edmund and try to talk him round.
To silence Edmund with the strychnine in his pocket.
To dine at home before going out.
To drink in the back parlour while waiting.
To go over the household books at home.
To reglaze the greenhouse frames before frost.
To stitch Rowan's cut hand.
To keep evening surgery hours.
To attend the collapsed man at the inn.
To run the taproom as usual.
To work late on papers, and to be seen there afterwards.
Word that brandy from her taproom killed Mr Vale will ruin the Rook & Lantern.
To put the brandy glass out of sight before anyone makes talk of it.
To leave his lamp lit and his hat and coat by the desk, so that anyone passing thinks he never left the vestry.
To walk his usual evening round of the churchyard.
Silas Voss was at his vestry desk all evening, because the lamp was lit and his hat and coat were by the desk.
Talk of irregular estate money will shame the Vale name in the village.
To lock Edmund's account notes in her writing box and say nothing of them.
To keep outsiders out of Edmund's study so no one asks about the estate money.
To leave word on the surgery slate so late patients know where she has gone.
To lock the back parlour and keep the key, so nothing is touched before the investigator sees it.
Mr Pike's cut is bleeding badly and she must reach him at once.
Mr Vale most likely died of a seizure, and a dead man's room is not to be opened for gossip or curiosity.
To take Mr Vale's body to the surgery's cold room overnight, out of the public inn.
The hatless man in a dark coat she glimpsed crossing the inn yard near twenty to ten was Rowan Pike in his green coat.
To keep her surgery day-book locked away, since it records patients' private complaints and the village feeds on such talk.
To keep the cold room locked so no one gawks at Mr Vale, and to open it only with his family's leave.
To know how Edmund really died, since he never had a fit or a seizure in his life.
To give the investigator written leave to see Edmund's body.
Dr Marsh knew what Clara's note said because Clara's leave-note was delivered to her at the surgery to authorize the examination of Edmund's body.
Raise the alarm on finding the body.

events.summary: Edmund and Clara dine together at the manor.
Clara works alone on the household books at the manor.
Edmund takes the back parlour and waits for Silas.
Silas works at his vestry office.
Silas arrives at the inn and orders nothing.
Edmund and Silas quarrel loudly over the estate accounts in the back parlour.
Edmund steps to the taproom for more brandy, then drinks it in the parlour.
Alone in the parlour a moment, Silas tips strychnine into Edmund's brandy glass, then leaves.
Edmund convulses and dies in the back parlour.
Silas returns to his vestry office and lights the lamp.
Rowan reglazes frames; at about 21:10 a pane slips and cuts his left hand.
Dr Marsh keeps evening surgery hours.
Dr Marsh stitches and bandages Rowan's hand at the greenhouse bench.
Rowan tidies the glass and stays at the greenhouse.
Dr Marsh, sent for, examines Edmund's body at the inn.
Ada serves in the taproom through the evening.
After Dr Marsh leaves, Ada takes Edmund's glass from the parlour and locks it in the cellar cupboard.
Ada closes up the taproom for the night.
Silas leaves the vestry lamp burning and hangs his hat and coat by the desk, then slips out.
Bell walks the churchyard round beside the vestry, glancing at its lit window.
Next morning Clara finds Edmund's account notes in his study desk and locks them in her writing box.
Clara locks Edmund's study door and hangs the key on her own chatelaine.
Dr Marsh chalks her departure on the door slate, but the chalk snaps on the hour, and she hurries out.
Bell locks the back parlour, pockets the key and tells Mrs Finch nobody goes in.
Dr Marsh quickly writes the greenhouse call in her surgery day-book and puts her watch down beside it.
Bell brings Edmund's body on a handcart from the inn and lays it in the surgery's cold back room.
Back from the inn, Dr Marsh shuts her day-book, locks it in her desk drawer and puts on her watch.
Once Bell has gone, Dr Marsh locks the cold back room and keeps the key on her own ring.
Clara writes and signs a short note giving the investigator leave to see Edmund's body.
Arthur Bell finds Edmund Vale dead and sends for the doctor.

signs.title: The doctor’s examination notes
signs.text: Examination of the deceased, Edmund Vale, reveals marked rigidity and discoloration consistent with a fast-acting poison taken by mouth. There is no external wound or blunt trauma upon the body. Death occurred between twenty-five past nine and quarter to ten, and I find nothing to suggest it came at any other hour.
signs.show: The doctor's notes say Edmund Vale was poisoned through a drink, with convulsions, and place his death between 21:25 and 21:45 last night. Does that match what you know?

reactions.silas: A grim finding, Inspector, but it tells you only how the man died, not who was near him. I was at my vestry office with my lamp lit, as anyone passing would have seen. I quarrelled with Edmund over accounts, yes — I've not hidden that — but a quarrel is not poison.

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Marsh on the body
signs.text: Death occurred between twenty-five past nine and quarter to ten, poor man — a poison taken by mouth, and it took him quickly, by the look of it. There's no mark of violence on him, so whatever he swallowed did its cruel work fast.
signs.ask: Doctor, what did you find when you examined Edmund?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says Edmund Vale died from a poison taken by mouth, sometime between twenty-five past nine and quarter to ten last night. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me Edmund Vale died from a poison taken by mouth, sometime between twenty-five past nine and quarter to ten last night. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the evening
signs.text: Did my usual round past the churchyard, saw the vestry window lit same as ever. Later I fetched Mr Vale's body over to the surgery and saw the back parlour locked up proper - nowt else to tell.
signs.confront: You told me you did your usual round, saw the vestry lit, and later found the parlour locked proper. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he did his usual churchyard round, saw the vestry window lit, and later found the back parlour locked proper after fetching Mr Vale's body. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the evening
signs.text: I kept my usual evening surgery, then was sent for from the inn once word came of Mr Vale's collapse. Between the two I saw to a hand injury at the greenhouse, and afterwards I settled my books and locked up as I always do.
signs.confront: You told me you kept surgery, saw to a hand at the greenhouse, then were called to the inn before locking up. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she kept her usual evening surgery, saw to a hand injury at the greenhouse, was called to the inn for Mr Vale, then went back and locked up as usual. Does that sound right to you?

signs.speaker: ada
signs.title: Ada Finch on the evening
signs.text: Oh, same as any night, love - I was run off my feet in the taproom serving through the evening, then I locked up after and went to my bed. Didn't have a moment to think of anything else, truly.
signs.confront: You told me you were run off your feet serving, then locked up and went to bed. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says she was busy serving in the taproom all evening, then locked up and went straight to bed. Do you know if that's true?

signs.speaker: silas
signs.title: Silas Voss on the evening
signs.text: I dined out and afterwards returned to my vestry office to work late on some papers. I lit the lamp and stayed at my desk into the evening.
signs.confront: You told me you dined out, then worked late at your desk in the vestry office. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Voss says he dined out, then returned to his vestry office and worked late at his desk by lamplight. Do you know if that's true?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the evening
signs.text: Was at the greenhouse, reglazing frames. Cut my hand on a pane, got it seen to, then stopped and tidied the glass. Was there the whole while.
signs.confront: You told me you were reglazing frames, cut your hand, had it seen to, and stayed at the greenhouse the whole while. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Pike says he was reglazing frames at the greenhouse, cut his hand on a pane, had it seen to, then tidied the glass and stayed put the whole while. Do you know if that's true?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the evening
signs.text: I was at the manor, seeing to the household books after dinner, and then I retired. There's little more to tell.
signs.confront: You told me you were seeing to the household books after dinner and then retired. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Miss Vale says she was at the manor going over the household books after dinner, then retired for the night. Do you know if that's true?

signs.title: Dr Marsh on the greenhouse
signs.text: After my last patient I went straight up to Mr Pike at the greenhouse. His left palm was laid open by glass. I stitched and bandaged it. He sat at the bench the whole time, and I was with him until I was fetched to the inn for Mr Vale. I'd left my watch behind, so I can't give you the hours.
signs.speaker: iris
signs.reading: The slate and the day-book show she left the surgery at nine. The greenhouse is about ten minutes' walk away, so she was with Mr Pike by about a quarter past, and she stayed until she was sent for after Mr Vale collapsed.
signs.ask: Dr Marsh, what can you tell me about the greenhouse?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she went straight to Mr Pike at the greenhouse after her last patient, stitched his cut palm, and stayed until called to the inn, though she can't give the hours. Does that match what happened, Mr Pike?
signs.confront: You told me Dr Marsh stitched your hand at the greenhouse and stayed with you until she was called away. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.silas: That is Dr Marsh's account and no concern of mine. My own evening was spent at the vestry over my papers, as Constable Bell will confirm.
reactions.rowan: Aye, that's right. Cut myself bad on the glass. Sat there the whole time she was stitching me, didn't move.
reactions.ada: Oh. Well, if the doctor was up at the greenhouse with him the whole while, then it can't have been Rowan I saw, can it. I was so sure it was him in that coat — I don't know who else it could've been, but I suppose I was wrong.

concede.s_surgery_slate: Ah — the slate. Yes, that would have been quarter past nine when I went up, and I stayed with him until quarter past ten, when I was fetched to the inn; I only said I couldn't give you the hours because I'd left my watch, not to muddy the matter.

signs.direct: Dr Marsh says she went straight to you at the greenhouse and stitched your left palm after it was laid open by glass. Is that so?

signs.title: The brandy glass
signs.text: Mr Vale's brandy glass, brought up from Mrs Finch's cellar cupboard. It has not been washed, and some dark dregs are left in it. When they are tested at the surgery, the dregs taste bitter and turn violet in the test for strychnine.
signs.unlock: Asked about the empty ring on the table, Mrs Finch goes red, admits she put the glass away so there'd be no talk, and brings it up from the locked cellar cupboard.
signs.show: This is Mr Vale's brandy glass from the cellar cupboard, unwashed with dark dregs that tested violet for strychnine - can you tell me anything about it?

reactions.ada: Oh, that's his glass right enough, I put it down cellar myself so no wagging tongues would start over the taproom brandy. I never touched what was in it, mind — I only wanted it out of sight till things settled. If there's poison in there, it's none of my doing, I swear it on the inn's good name.
reactions.silas: That is unfortunate, but it proves nothing beyond what the doctor already told you — the glass sat unwashed in a cellar overnight. I poured Mr Vale no drink and mixed him nothing. You will need more than dregs to hang a man.

signs.title: The parlour table
signs.text: The back parlour has been left much as it was found. The brandy decanter stands on the table, and beside Mr Vale's chair there is a dried, sticky ring where a glass stood. There is no glass on the table, the floor or the sideboard.
signs.unlock: Constable Bell walks you to the Rook & Lantern and unlocks the back parlour with his key.
signs.show: There's a dried, sticky ring on the parlour table beside Mr Vale's chair where a glass must have stood, yet no glass can be found anywhere in the room - what happened to it?

signs.title: Constable Bell on the vestry
signs.text: Walked the churchyard round from twenty past nine till near twenty to ten. Vestry lamp was lit the whole while. Mr Voss's hat and coat were by his desk, same as always. He was at his papers. I'd swear to it.
signs.speaker: bell
signs.ask: Constable Bell, what did you notice about the vestry?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he walked the churchyard from twenty past nine till near twenty to ten and saw Mr Voss at his papers in the lit vestry the whole time. Would you agree with that account?
signs.confront: You told me you saw Mr Voss at his papers in the vestry the whole time you walked the churchyard, from twenty past nine till near twenty to ten. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.silas: Just so. I kept to my papers, and the constable's round confirms it — as I told you, I never left the vestry that evening.

signs.direct: Constable Bell says your hat and coat were by your desk and you were at your papers while he walked the churchyard. Is that so?

signs.title: Mrs Finch on the back parlour
signs.text: Mr Voss came in about twenty to nine and never ordered a drop. He and Mr Vale went at it in the parlour till near half past nine. Mr Vale came out for more brandy, and Mr Voss was still sat in there. He went out the side door a bit after. Twenty to ten, I'd say.
signs.speaker: ada
signs.unlock: With the glass out and no more point in keeping quiet for the inn's sake, Mrs Finch tells you everything she saw in the parlour.
signs.ask: Mrs Finch, what did you find in the back parlour?
signs.confront: Mrs Finch says you came in around twenty to nine, ordered nothing, argued with Mr Vale in the parlour till half past nine, and left by the side door about twenty to ten. Is that right?

reactions.silas: Mrs Finch is mistaken, or has muddled her evening. I do not deny Edmund and I exchanged words over the accounts, but I returned directly to the vestry and worked, as Bell will attest.
reactions.bell: Aye, well. I told it as I saw it — lamp lit, hat and coat by the desk, and I took that for him at his papers. If Mrs Finch had him in the parlour till near half past nine, then I were wrong about the lamp meaning aught. I'll not argue with what she saw plain.

signs.show: Mrs Finch says Mr Voss arrived without ordering a drink and argued with Mr Vale in the back parlour until about half past nine, leaving by the side door near twenty to ten. Does that match what you know?
signs.direct: Mrs Finch says you argued with Mr Vale in the parlour until half past nine and were still seated there when he fetched more brandy, before you left by the side door around twenty to ten. Is that so?

signs.title: Edmund's notes on the accounts
signs.text: Foolscap sheets in Mr Vale's hand. Two columns: ledger entries for roof repairs, drainage and seed, all written in Mr Voss's hand, set against the bank passbook. Each sum was drawn out, but beside it Mr Vale has written 'no work done' or 'never delivered'. At the foot: 'Two years. Paid to S.V.'s own account at Hartley's. Have it out with him.'
signs.unlock: When you tell Miss Vale that Mrs Finch heard the quarrel over the accounts and the whole village will soon know of it, she sees there is no point keeping quiet any longer and takes the notes from her writing box.
signs.show: These are Mr Vale's notes comparing ledger entries in Mr Voss's hand against the bank passbook, marking sums as 'no work done' and noting payments to Mr Voss's own account at Hartley's - what can you tell me about this?

reactions.silas: Mr Vale kept careless notes, and careless men draw careless conclusions. The accounts were mine to manage and I answer for every entry, not for his private scribbling. I'll not be condemned on the strength of a dead man's marginalia.
reactions.clara: Yes, I found those papers and locked them away — they concern estate business, not murder, and I saw no reason to air the family's affairs before I understood them myself. I should have shown you sooner; I'm sorry for that.

signs.title: Miss Vale and the study
signs.text: Mr Vale's study door is locked. The key hangs on Miss Vale's chatelaine. When you ask to look inside, she says there is nothing there that concerns anyone and changes the subject. While she speaks, she looks twice at the writing box on her side table, which is also locked.
signs.show: Miss Vale keeps Mr Vale's study locked and carries the key herself. When I asked to look inside, she brushed it off and kept glancing at the locked writing box on her table. Have you noticed her acting this way?
signs.confront: You keep the study locked and brushed off my question about it, glancing twice at your locked writing box. What is it you're not telling me?

reactions.clara: I locked the study because Edmund's papers are not for idle eyes, not because I have anything to hide from you. The writing box holds nothing but what I've already given you notice of — his notes on the accounts.

signs.direct: You keep your brother's study locked and brushed off my question about it, while glancing twice at your own locked writing box. Can you explain that?

signs.title: The surgery door slate
signs.text: A small chalk slate hangs by the surgery door. In a quick, neat hand it says: 'Left   o'clock for greenhouse — Mr Pike, cut hand. I.M.' Where the hour should be there is only a short stroke and a white smear. A snapped end of chalk lies on the step below.
signs.reading: The day-book's last entry is the greenhouse call at nine. So the smeared hour on the slate is nine, which is when she went out of the door.
signs.show: This slate by the surgery door notes you left for the greenhouse to see Mr Pike's cut hand, but the hour is smeared away and there's a broken chalk end on the step - can you explain that?

reactions.iris: Yes, that's my slate and my hand, though the chalk failed me on the hour — I was in too much haste over Mr Pike's hand to mind it. I can't give you the exact time from that smear, only that I left as soon as I was sent for.

signs.direct: Dr Marsh's slate says she left to see to your cut hand, but the hour is smeared out and there's a snapped chalk end on the step. Can you tell me what time that really was?

signs.title: Constable Bell's key
signs.text: Locked the inn's back parlour myself last night, once the doctor was done. Key's in my pocket. Wasn't opening it for gossip. Arched like that, though... that's no fit. Nobody's been in. I'll walk you over and open it.
signs.speaker: bell
signs.unlock: When you describe the state of the body to Constable Bell, he stops treating the death as a fit and agrees to open the parlour he sealed.
signs.ask: Constable Bell, what can you tell me about the key?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he locked the inn's back parlour himself once the doctor was done, and he's certain nobody's been in since, though he thought the door's arched fitting looked wrong. Do you know anything about that?
signs.confront: You told me you locked the back parlour yourself and that nobody's been in since. What did you mean about the arched fitting not being right?

signs.title: The surgery day-book
signs.text: Dr Marsh takes the surgery day-book from her locked desk drawer and opens it at last night. She says her wristwatch was lying beside it when she came back. The last lines are in a neat hand: '8.40 — last evening patient, dressing changed.' Under that: '9.0 — sent for to greenhouse, R. Pike, glass cut to palm. Went at once.' Nothing is written after it.
signs.unlock: When you tell Dr Marsh that Mrs Finch is putting Mr Pike at the inn at twenty to ten, she unlocks her desk drawer and shows you the day-book so her patient is not wrongly accused.
signs.show: The surgery day-book shows Dr Marsh was called away to the greenhouse at nine for R. Pike's cut hand, with no entries after that, and her wristwatch was left lying beside it. Does that match your understanding of her movements?

reactions.iris: That's my day-book, kept as I always keep it, and those entries are accurate as far as they go. I set my watch beside it when I wrote them and put it back on when I returned — nothing after that concerns the greenhouse call.

signs.direct: Your day-book stops after you record being sent to the greenhouse at nine for Mr Pike's cut, with your watch left lying beside it. Can you explain the gap after that?

signs.title: The body in the back room
signs.text: Mr Vale lies under a sheet in the cold back room of the surgery. His back is stiffly arched and his fists are clenched. His jaw is locked in a fixed grin. The heels of his shoes are scuffed raw, as though they drummed hard against the floorboards.
signs.reading: Strychnine causes convulsions before death. The arched back, locked jaw and drummed heels are signs of those convulsions, not of a quiet heart failure or an ordinary fit.
signs.unlock: Dr Marsh keeps the cold room locked against gawkers. She reads Miss Vale's note, nods, and unlocks the door for you.
signs.show: Mr Vale's body shows a stiffly arched back, clenched fists, a fixed grin, and heels scuffed raw as if they'd drummed against the floor - can you help me understand what caused this?

reactions.bell: Aye, I laid him there myself, off the handcart. Didn't much like the look of him then, and I like it less now — that arching and the grin weren't natural for a seizure, to my mind. Best the doctor makes sense of it, that's not my trade.

signs.title: Mrs Finch on a man in the yard
signs.text: I'll tell you what I saw, and I'm sure of it. About twenty to ten a man went across the inn yard, no hat on, dark coat, in a tearing hurry. That was Rowan Pike in that green coat of his. Everyone's talking about it. What he wanted round here that time of night, I couldn't say.
signs.speaker: ada
signs.ask: Mrs Finch, what did you see of a man in the yard?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says she saw a man in a dark coat, no hat, hurrying across the inn yard about twenty to ten, and she's certain it was Rowan Pike in his green coat. Can you account for that, Mr Pike?
signs.confront: Mrs Finch says she saw you hurrying across the inn yard around twenty to ten, hatless, in your green coat. What were you doing there at that hour?

reactions.rowan: Weren't me. I was up at the greenhouse the whole time, hand cut open, doctor stitching me. Ask her yourself.

signs.direct: Mrs Finch says she saw you hurrying across the inn yard about twenty to ten, no hat, in your green coat. Is that so?

signs.title: Constable Bell on the death
signs.text: Fit, most like. Mr Vale took bad in the inn parlour and went before the doctor got there. I carted him to the surgery's back room last night. No sense in folk gawking at him. Doctor has the room locked now. That's the end of it, far as I'm concerned.
signs.speaker: bell
signs.ask: Constable Bell, what did you observe about Mr Vale's death?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he took it for a fit, that Mr Vale collapsed in the inn parlour before the doctor arrived, and that he carried him to the surgery's back room himself. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me you thought it was a fit, that Mr Vale collapsed in the inn parlour, and that you carried him to the surgery's back room yourself. Is that truly the end of it?

signs.title: Miss Vale's note
signs.text: A short note on Vale Manor paper, in a small upright hand: 'Dr Marsh, please allow the bearer to see my brother. C. Vale.' The ink is fresh.
signs.unlock: When you tell Miss Vale the constable is calling it a fit, she says quietly that Edmund never had a fit in his life. She writes a note so that you can see him.
signs.show: This note on Vale Manor paper, signed by you, asks Dr Marsh to let the bearer see your brother, and the ink looks quite fresh - can you tell me about it?

reactions.clara: Yes, that's my hand and my leave. See him, if it helps you find what happened — he never had a seizure in his life, whatever anyone says.

signs.direct: You wrote this note asking Dr Marsh to let the bearer see your brother, and the ink is still fresh. Can you tell me more about it?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.unlock: once you have The surgery door slate, you can ask Rowan Pike about it
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the surgery door slate
signs.text: That's just where Dr Marsh chalked she'd gone to see to my hand at the greenhouse. I keep glazing tools out there and a pane caught me, nothing more to it.
signs.ask: This slate mentions your cut hand, Mr Pike - do you know anything about it?
signs.show: Mr Pike says the surgery slate was just Dr Marsh noting she'd gone to see to his cut hand at the greenhouse, from a pane that caught him while glazing. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me the slate was simply Dr Marsh noting she'd gone to tend your cut hand at the greenhouse, from a pane that caught you glazing. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.unlock: once you have Miss Vale's note, you can ask Dr Iris Marsh about it
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on miss vale's note
signs.text: She sent it round so whoever was asking could be let in to see him properly, that's all - I keep such notes with the day-book once they've served their purpose.
signs.ask: Miss Vale wrote this note allowing someone to see her brother's body - do you know why it came to you?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says Miss Vale's note was sent so whoever was asking could be let in to see Mr Vale properly, and that she keeps such notes with the day-book afterward. Does that match what you understood?
signs.confront: You told me Miss Vale's note was meant to let the bearer in to see Mr Vale properly, and that you keep such notes with the day-book. Is that the whole of it?

title: The Back Parlour
synopsis: Edmund Vale collapsed and died in the back parlour of the Rook & Lantern.

clara: I keep the manor's household keys on my chatelaine, as I always have.
I understand it was Rowan who raised the alarm this morning and that word was sent for Dr Marsh and Constable Bell.
rowan: I live and keep my tools in the greenhouse, which is where I spend most of my working hours.
My hand's bandaged and folk have been asking after it, and I know Dr Marsh saw to it.
silas: I keep my papers and a spare set of estate documents locked in my vestry office.
ada: I run the Rook & Lantern, the village inn, and see to the taproom and the rooms above.
I live at the inn and keep the taproom, cellar and till keys myself.
iris: I keep the surgery and its cold room locked, and I hold the only keys to them.
bell: I'm the village constable, keeping order and walking my rounds about the square and churchyard.
I know everyone in the village in the course of my duties - Clara, Rowan, Silas, Ada and Dr Marsh all included.

moods.rowan: Sore-handed and a bit subdued, but focused on getting the greenhouse frames fixed before the cold sets in.
moods.silas: Simply going about his day, tired and a little saddened by the news in the village.
